extracted.subtask_description: Methods, solution strategies, and worked solutions for algebra and analysis problems from mathematical-olympiad style contests (inequalities, functional equations, matrices, mean-value-theorem applications, combinatorics).

rubrics_metrics.name: without_loss_of_generality_ordering
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume an ordering of variables (e.g., x1 ≤ x2 ≤ · · · ≤ xn) 'without loss of generality' to simplify comparisons and sign information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text example: 'We may assume, without loss of generality, that x1 ≤ x2 ≤ · · · ≤ xn, so xi − xi+1 ≤ 0 ...' Use WLOG orderings to fix monotonicity and reduce casework; justify that permutations do not affect the property to be proved.

rubrics_metrics.name: apply_abel_summation_formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Transform sums of ratios or weighted sums by applying Abel summation (partial summation) to obtain alternative expressions suitable for bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text example: 'Consider the sum ∑_{i=1}^n xi/ui and apply the Abel summation formula to obtain ∑_{i=1}^{n−1} Ui(xi − xi+1) + Un xn.' Use this to convert ∑ xi/ui into telescoping-like terms multiplied by cumulative quantities Ui.

rubrics_metrics.name: use_am-gm_inequality_for_bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the AM–GM inequality to obtain lower or upper bounds on sums or to deduce simple inequalities like x + 1/x > 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple uses in text: 'Now, by the AM–GM inequality, n ≥ ∑ xi/ui ≥ n n (x1x2···xn / u1u2···un)'. Use AM–GM to compare arithmetic and geometric means and derive contradictions or bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: proof_by_induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove statements for all n by establishing base case(s) and deriving a recurrence or inductive step that uses previous cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text examples: 'The conclusion of the problem follows by induction from the identity ...', and several problems use induction on n to propagate polynomial identities or inequalities. Include base-case checking and demonstrating how n → n+1 follows.

rubrics_metrics.name: express_powers_via_polynomial_identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Express x^{m} + 1/x^{m} as a polynomial in x + 1/x (or similar reductions) to obtain recurrences or reduce exponent problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example identity: 'x^2 + 1/x^2 = (x + 1/x)^2 − 2' and the recurrence for odd exponents: x^{2n+1} − 1/x^{2n+1} = (x^2 + 1/x^2)·(x^{2n−1} − 1/x^{2n−1}) − ...'. Use these to reduce large exponents to functions of x + 1/x.

rubrics_metrics.name: use_triangle_similarity_and_trig_relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit triangle similarity, angle bisectors, and the law of sines to convert geometric configurations into algebraic/trigonometric relations (e.g., obtain golden ratio from a pentagonal angle configuration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text example: analyze triangle with angles π/5, 2π/5, 2π/5, use CD as bisector, deduce AB/BC = (1+√5)/2, then apply law of sines: AB/BC = sin C / sin A = 2 cos(π/5). Use geometry→similarity→trig chain to get exact algebraic values.

rubrics_metrics.name: use_complex_numbers_and_roots_of_unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Model trigonometric expressions with complex numbers z = cos θ + i sin θ and use powers/roots of unity to deduce rationality/irrationality or evaluate cos(kθ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text example: 'Let z = cos 1° + i sin 1°. Since z + 1/z = 2 cos 1° is rational, z^{45} + 1/z^{45} = 2 cos 45° = 2, contradiction.' Use multiplicative properties of complex exponentials to lift rationality information.

rubrics_metrics.name: factorization_and_polynomial_recursions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use factorizations and polynomial recurrences to deduce divisibility or integrality properties (e.g., proving integer divisibility by powers of 2 via recursion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: derive recursion bn = 8bn−1 − 4bn−2 or show bn equals c_n^2 where c_n satisfies c_n = 10 c_{n−1} − c_{n−2}. Use recurrences plus base values to deduce arithmetic divisibility/integrality properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: apply_mean_value_theorem_and_rolles_theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Rolle's theorem / the Mean Value Theorem to prove existence/uniqueness, to equate derivatives at different points, or to bound function differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text examples: multiple problems in Section 2.10 apply MVT or Rolle to show uniqueness of solutions, derive identities like f'(c)/f(c) = (ln f(b) − ln f(a))/(b − a), or deduce contradictions by producing equal internal points in disjoint intervals. Use MVT to translate differences into derivatives at intermediate points.

rubrics_metrics.name: pigeonhole_principle_and_ordering_arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Use pigeonhole principle and ordering/arrangement of numbers or geometric pieces to force repetitions or existence of desired structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: cutting plane into regions by lines corresponding to orderings (six pieces for x,y,z), or counting sequences and ranges to force equalities (e.g., ai + a1 versus aj − a2). Use ordering to convert combinatorial constraints into forced matches.

rubrics_metrics.name: arrange_increasing_order_and_compare_differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange sequences in increasing order and study consecutive differences or cumulative sums to derive inequalities or existence statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple solutions begin 'Arrange the numbers in increasing order a1 ≤ a2 ≤ ...' then analyze differences a_{k+1} − a_k or partial sums s_i to partition sums and obtain contradictions or constructive arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: use_determinant_identities_and_spectral_arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: In matrix problems, use determinant identities (e.g., det(I − AB) = det(I − BA)), block-matrix factorizations, Cayley–Hamilton theorem, and spectral mapping to deduce invertibility or determinant sign properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text demonstrates writing block matrices as products to relate determinants, applying Cayley–Hamilton (p(B)=0), and spectral mapping to show invertibility of A + I. Also uses |det(A + iI)|^2 ≥ 0 to show det(A^2 + I) ≥ 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: completing_square_or_cube_for_number_theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete the square or cube to rewrite expressions as (something)^2 ± const or (something)^3 ± const to analyze perfect-square/cube properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: k(k+1)(k+2)(k+3) = (k^2 + 3k + 1)^2 − 1 to show not a square; complete cube in other problems to bound closeness to perfect powers. Use this to sandwich quantities between consecutive powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: use_modular_arithmetic_and_fermat_little_theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply congruences and basic number-theoretic results (e.g., Fermat's little theorem) to reduce problems modulo primes and obtain contradictions or necessary equalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example in Section 2.10 problem 3: 'Fermat's little theorem implies ap − a ≡ 0 (mod p)...' then use inequalities to conclude required relations. Use modular reductions to force distinctions between sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: construct_counterexamples_and_sharp_examples
rubrics_metrics.description: When asked for existence/nonexistence or sharpness, present explicit counterexamples or constructions (e.g., {33,34,...,100} as a counterexample).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text gives constructive counterexample sets to show a claim fails, or constructs explicit sequences/numbers (via multiplication by perfect squares) to meet digit constraints. Use direct construction to disprove universal statements or to show optimality.

rubrics_metrics.name: extremal_principle_and_infimum_arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Use extremal/minimality arguments (choose infimum or minimum t0) together with continuity and MVT to derive contradictions or show global properties (e.g., derivative constant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: define M = {t ≥ 0 | f'(t) = f'(x)}, let t0 = inf M; use continuity and MVT on [t0/2, t0] to contradict minimality unless t0 = 0. Use extremal choice to force structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: squeeze_principle_for_limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Bound a sequence/function between two sequences/functions that converge to the same limit to deduce the original limit via the squeezing (sandwich) principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: bounding n f'(c_n) between expressions tending to 0 and invoking limits of related elementary functions (like (1+1/n)^n → e) to conclude the target limit is 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: use_recursions_and_sequence_identifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce auxiliary sequences via linear recurrences (bn, cn, etc.), identify closed forms or relations (e.g., bn = c_n^2), and use induction on recurrences to prove integrality/divisibility properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text: define bn = (an + 1)/6, derive bn+1 = 98bn − bn−1 − 16 and show bn = c_n^2 where c_n satisfies c_n = 10 c_{n−1} − c_{n−2}. Prove equality by checking initial terms and inductive step.
